headline: Florida wins projects. It does not win large productive capital.
summary: Compared with 10 competing states, Florida lands many corporate facility projects and its manufacturing base is growing, but per resident it captures far less factory, lab and megaproject capital. The gap is real, sector-specific and measurable; the claim that Florida gets no business investment is false.

measures.label: Corporate facility projects per million residents
measures.question: How many projects?
measures.read: Florida recorded 326 qualifying projects, 5th by count, but ranked 31st per resident. It ranked 42nd per resident in 2022.
measures.caveat: Counts projects meeting any of $1 million, 20 jobs or 20,000 square feet; measures breadth, not dollars.

measures.label: Manufacturing capital spending per resident
measures.question: What did manufacturers actually spend?
measures.read: Manufacturers spent $5.11 billion on plant and equipment in Florida. Relative to its own manufacturing output Florida reinvests at about a typical rate, so the gap is mostly the size of its manufacturing base. Aerospace is the exception: about 16% of U.S. aerospace capital spending.
measures.caveat: Covers manufacturing establishments only, not data centers. The 2024 estimate is experimental; the 2022 Economic Census shows the same low position.

measures.label: Announced $1B+ project capital per resident, excluding data centers and LNG
measures.question: Where are the billion-dollar projects going?
measures.read: Florida's 3 active projects total $3.84 billion. Virginia, the lowest of the 10 competitors, is about 13 times Florida's figure per resident.
measures.caveat: Announced multi-year totals at the latest disclosure, not spending. The $1 billion threshold leaves out Florida wins between $250 million and $1 billion. Single projects dominate some totals: SpaceX Vermilion Parish spaceport is 72% of Louisiana's; Intel Ohio One is 68% of Ohio's; TSMC Arizona semiconductor campus is 84% of Arizona's. The inventory is systematic but not proven complete.

measures.label: Share of U.S. planned foreign greenfield investment
measures.question: Do foreign investors build here?
measures.read: Foreign investors planned $2.26 billion of new or expanded facilities in Florida, while spending $22.6 billion to acquire existing Florida businesses.
measures.caveat: Foreign investors only. BEA assigns each investment to the state with the most employees and suppresses some cells; greenfield figures are planned totals.

measures.label: Manufacturing employment change
measures.question: Contrary evidence: is the base shrinking?
measures.read: Florida added manufacturing jobs while the nation lost them. The thesis holds for large productive capital, not for business activity in general.
measures.caveat: Annual averages of monthly state estimates; employment change is not attributable to any single project.

measures.label: Jobs added by newly opened business locations, per 100 private-sector jobs a year
measures.question: Contrary evidence: do new businesses open here, and do they last?
measures.read: Florida both opens and closes business locations faster than any competitor: closings cost 6.2 jobs per 100 (4th-highest of 50), so openings net of closings add 0.5, against 0.3 nationally. Most of Florida's faster job growth (2.1 per 100 a year against 1.3) comes from established employers shedding fewer jobs.
measures.caveat: Private sector, seasonally adjusted; the four quarterly rates are summed for each year. Openings include new locations of existing firms and seasonal reopenings, so tourism-heavy states run higher. These are jobs, not investment.

measures.label: Average private-sector pay
measures.question: Contrary evidence: are the jobs getting better paid?
measures.read: Florida's private-sector jobs paid 92% of the national average in 2025, up from 86% in 2019. Only 3 states raised average pay faster since 2019 (+42% against +34% nationally).
measures.caveat: Annual averages in nominal dollars; the latest year is subject to revision. Averages move with the mix of jobs as well as with raises, so this signals job quality; it does not measure productivity.

dataCenters.headline: The AI data-center build-out has not reached Florida.

facts.label: Hyperscale data-center campuses in Florida
facts.read: None operating, under construction or announced as of September 25, 2026. Florida's hyperscaler footprint is network and edge infrastructure, such as Google's Palm Coast cable hub and an AWS Local Zone in Miami.

facts.label: Signed large-load data-center contracts announced by FPL or Duke Energy Florida
facts.read: Duke Energy Florida testified in April 2026 that it has no large-load data-center customers. FPL reported more than 20 GW of inquiries but had announced no signed contract by July 24, 2026.

facts.label: 2026 capital-spending guidance, four largest cloud companies
facts.read: Company-wide and global. None of it is allocated to states, so no Florida share can be computed.

facts.label: Largest Florida data-center proposals
facts.read: The $2.84 billion Fort Meade proposal (end user undisclosed) is contested and not permitted; Palm Beach County denied Project Tango in July 2026.

dataCenters.caveat: Leases and colocation contracts are often confidential; absence of public evidence is not proof of absence. Undisclosed end users are not attributed.

finalists.headline: Florida is rarely in the final round for billion-dollar projects.
finalists.read: Florida was not a finalist for any $1B+ project whose competing sites are on the public record. Texas incentive filings name rival sites for 20 of 27 billion-dollar projects: Louisiana appears in 8, New Mexico in 5 and Florida in 1, only on Saronic's 12-state first-round list. Apart from that first-round exit, Florida's 13 documented contest losses since 2020 are mid-sized, including Boom Supersonic (Jacksonville), Pratt & Whitney (Palm Beach County), Jabil and Citi's technology hub to North Carolina and a Miami-Dade steel-mill site that was one of three finalists (Texas won).
finalists.caveat: North Carolina and Texas publish the alternative locations applicants name, so contests lost to those states are over-represented; most states publish none, and some Texas applicants keep their alternatives confidential.

method: Announced commitments are not spending, and an opening does not prove the full budget was spent or every job filled.
Per-resident figures use Census Vintage 2025 population; values are nominal dollars.
Agency-reported totals use incompatible scopes and are not compared here.
Company-wide hyperscaler capital spending is never allocated to states.
BLS job-flow and pay measures describe private-sector jobs, not investment; they test whether the gap is general or specific to large capital.
